A hipster is a person — usually a young adult — who deliberately avoids mainstream, popular culture and instead seeks out things that feel underground, indie, obscure, or alternative. The driving belief of a hipster is that mass-market, commercially popular things are shallow or soulless, and that true taste means discovering things before they become popular, or rejecting them because they already are.

A hipster is defined by a very specific combination of attitudes, tastes, and aesthetics that all add up to one central desire: to seem authentic and non-conformist.

Taste in music and art: Hipsters gravitate toward indie bands, underground musicians, and artists that most people haven't heard of. They often lose interest in a band once it becomes mainstream — the fact that "everyone likes them now" is itself a reason to move on. The obscurity of their taste is treated as a badge of honor.

Food and drink culture: Hipsters are deeply associated with artisanal and craft everything — craft beer, single-origin pour-over coffee, small-batch hot sauce, sourdough bread made from scratch. They care deeply about where food comes from (local farms, organic produce), how it's made, and whether it has a "story" behind it. A corporate chain coffee shop is the opposite of what a hipster finds acceptable; a tiny, independent café where the barista explains the flavor notes of your coffee like a sommelier? Perfect.

Fashion and appearance: The hipster look is very recognizable, which is ironic given their desire to stand out:

  • Thick-rimmed glasses (often without prescription lenses — purely as a style choice)
  • Vintage or thrift-store clothing — old flannel shirts, faded denim, retro sneakers
  • Beanies, scarves, and layered outfits
  • For men: full, carefully groomed beards; for women: minimal or "effortlessly natural" makeup
  • General aesthetic: looks deliberately unstudied, even though considerable effort went into it

Hobbies and interests: Vinyl records over digital music. Film cameras over digital. Typewriters over laptops. Bicycles (especially fixed-gear bikes) over cars. DIY crafts, zines, urban gardening, local farmers' markets. The older, more handmade, or more "analog" a thing is, the more a hipster tends to value it.

Values: Hipsters typically hold progressive political views — environmentalism, support for local and independent businesses, opposition to large corporations, awareness of social issues. These aren't fake or superficial values; they're genuine, but they're also tied up with identity and image in a way that makes it hard to separate the belief from the aesthetic.

Here is the most important thing to understand about the word "hipster," and what gives it its satirical edge:

Hipsters are non-conformists who all ended up conforming to the same non-conformist template.

Every hipster, trying to be unique and different from the mainstream crowd, ended up wearing the same glasses, drinking the same coffee, listening to the same kinds of obscure bands, and shopping at the same type of vintage stores — as every other hipster. They rejected one mass culture and accidentally created a new, very recognizable one of their own.

This is why the word "hipster" is almost always used with a knowing smirk. It captures a specific form of irony: the earnest, intense pursuit of authenticity that somehow produces a highly predictable, packaged identity.
How the Word Is Used in Tone

The word "hipster" is rarely used as a compliment and is almost never used by someone to describe themselves — because doing so would destroy the very image they're trying to project. If you're trying to be a hipster, you're already failing at it, by their own logic.

It is most commonly used:

  • As gentle mockery or teasing: "He only listens to bands no one's heard of — total hipster."
  • As a mild insult: "That café is too hipster for me — they charge ₹600 for a coffee and there's no Wi-Fi."
  • Descriptively, without strong judgment: "The neighborhood has really changed — it's become very hipster, lots of independent bookshops and artisan bakeries."
  • Self-deprecatingly: Occasionally someone will call themselves a hipster with self-aware humor, acknowledging the irony.

Hipster culture is strongly urban and strongly tied to specific neighborhoods within big cities. Think of the artsy, gentrifying parts of a major city — areas that used to be industrial or working-class but have become home to young, educated, creative types. The classic examples are Williamsburg in Brooklyn (New York), Shoreditch in London, Kreuzberg in Berlin, or the Mission District in San Francisco. Many Indian cities now have their own equivalents — pockets of Bangalore, Mumbai, or Delhi with independent cafés, street art, and vintage clothing stores that carry the same energy.
Who Tends to Be Called a Hipster?

Typically: educated young adults (20s to early 30s), often from middle-class or upper-middle-class backgrounds, working in creative fields like design, photography, writing, music, or tech. The hipster identity requires a certain amount of money (artisanal goods aren't cheap) and leisure time, even as it often performs a kind of working-class or bohemian aesthetic.
The Relationship Between Hipsters and Trends

There's a classic cycle worth understanding:

  1. Hipsters discover something obscure — a neighborhood, a food, a style, a band.
  2. It slowly becomes known because hipsters talk about it.
  3. It enters mainstream culture and becomes widely popular.
  4. Hipsters abandon it, saying it's "sold out" or "too mainstream now."
  5. They move on to find the next obscure thing.

This cycle means hipsters are, paradoxically, one of the biggest drivers of mainstream trends — even as they define themselves by rejecting the mainstream. Cold brew coffee, avocado toast, craft beer, vinyl records, and artisanal everything all entered mainstream culture largely through this pipeline. Hipsters discover; the mainstream adopts; hipsters move on.

If you want to boil it all the way down: a hipster is someone who makes a lifestyle and identity out of being alternative, indie, and anti-mainstream — valuing things for their authenticity, craft, and obscurity — while being largely unaware that this very pursuit has made them part of a highly recognizable, somewhat self-contradictory subculture.

The word captures both a real cultural phenomenon and a mild joke about human nature — our desire to be unique, and how that desire, when shared by thousands of people, creates its own kind of conformity.
